title: Install WSL2 + Ubuntu 24.04 on Windows
why: Your Windows laptop becomes a Linux workstation. Open PowerShell as Administrator. Reboot when asked, then open 'Ubuntu' from the Start menu and create a Linux user.
code:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04
wsl --set-default-version 2
wsl -l -v        # should show Ubuntu-24.04  VERSION 2
expect: Ubuntu-24.04 listed with VERSION 2. Also install Windows Terminal and VS Code with the 'WSL' extension; open your lab folder with `code .` from Ubuntu.

title: Base tools inside Ubuntu (WSL)
why: Everything below runs in the Ubuntu terminal, not PowerShell.
code:
sudo apt update && sudo apt -y upgrade
sudo apt install -y build-essential git curl wget jq unzip tree python3-venv python3-pip \
  sysstat stress-ng fio iperf3 ethtool numactl hwloc pciutils htop tmux
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

title: Docker, kind, kubectl, helm, k9s
why: Install Docker Desktop for Windows and enable Settings > Resources > WSL integration > Ubuntu-24.04. Then install the Kubernetes CLIs inside Ubuntu.
code:
docker run --rm hello-world            # proves Docker works from WSL

# kubectl
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -Ls https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl && rm kubectl
# kind (check https://kind.sigs.k8s.io for the latest version)
curl -Lo kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/v0.27.0/kind-linux-amd64 && sudo install kind /usr/local/bin/kind && rm kind
# helm
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
# k9s (optional, nice UI)
curl -sS https://webinstall.dev/k9s | bash

kind create cluster --name lab && kubectl get nodes
expect: `kubectl get nodes` shows `lab-control-plane   Ready`. Delete it with `kind delete cluster --name lab` when done.

title: AWS sandbox account with guard-rails (do this before any GPU)
why: Use a separate AWS account (or one only for this lab), never a customer account. In the console: (1) MFA on root and lock it away. (2) Billing > Budgets > create a monthly cost budget of $50 with email alerts at 50%, 80%, 100%. (3) Create an IAM Identity Center user or an IAM user with AdministratorAccess for the lab only. (4) Pick one region and stay in it (us-east-1 or us-west-2 have the most GPU capacity; ap-south-1 is fine for g4dn/g5).
code:
# AWS CLI v2 + Session Manager plugin (lets you log in to instances with no SSH port open)
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o awscliv2.zip && unzip -q awscliv2.zip && sudo ./aws/install && rm -rf aws awscliv2.zip
curl "https://s3.amazonaws.com/session-manager-downloads/plugin/latest/ubuntu_64bit/session-manager-plugin.deb" -o smp.deb && sudo dpkg -i smp.deb && rm smp.deb
aws configure sso        # or: aws configure  (access key of the lab-only user)
aws sts get-caller-identity
expect: `get-caller-identity` prints your lab account ID. A budget email confirmation arrives.

title: Request GPU quota (takes 1-3 days - do it on day 1)
why: New accounts usually have 0 vCPU for GPU instances. Request: 'Running On-Demand G and VT instances' = 48 and 'All G and VT Spot Instance Requests' = 48 (enough for one g4dn.12xlarge). Later, if you need p-instances, request 'Running On-Demand P instances'. Quota codes below are what AWS uses today - confirm in Service Quotas > Amazon EC2 if a call fails.
code:
aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-DB2E81BA   # On-Demand G and VT
aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-3819A6DF   # Spot G and VT
aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-DB2E81BA --desired-value 48
aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-3819A6DF --desired-value 48
expect: Requests show as PENDING, then APPROVED by email. While waiting, do the laptop labs (A1, B1, K1, D1, G1, H4).

title: Install Terraform and create your portfolio repo
why: Everything you build goes into one Git repo. This is what you show in interviews.
code:
wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y terraform

mkdir -p ~/gpu-lab && cd ~/gpu-lab && git init
mkdir -p infra/{vms,gpu1,efa2} linux gpu-health topology bmc rdma nccl slurm k8s cloud observability llm capstone notes results
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# GPU Bring-up Lab
Hands-on journal for GPU infrastructure (NVIDIA SA Infrastructure prep).
Each folder = one domain. Each lab = script + results/ + notes/<lab>.md (what I did, what broke, what I learned).
EOF
git add . && git commit -m "lab skeleton"
expect: `tree -L 1 ~/gpu-lab` shows the folders. Create a private GitHub repo and push; make it public later once polished.

title: Terraform: two small Linux VMs (environment V)
why: Save as ~/gpu-lab/infra/vms/main.tf. Uses the default VPC, Ubuntu 24.04, SSM login (no SSH port), a security group that allows all traffic between the two VMs (needed for RDMA/iperf), and a 6-hour self-destruct as a safety net.
expect: Run: `cd ~/gpu-lab/infra/vms && terraform init && terraform apply`. Log in with `aws ssm start-session --target <id>` then `sudo -iu ubuntu`. Destroy with `terraform destroy` at the end of every session.

title: Terraform: one GPU spot instance (environment G1 / G4)
why: Save as ~/gpu-lab/infra/gpu1/main.tf. Uses the AWS Deep Learning Base GPU AMI (NVIDIA driver, CUDA, Docker + NVIDIA container toolkit, EFA, NCCL already installed), spot pricing, SSM login and a 4-hour self-destruct. Change instance_type to g4dn.12xlarge for G4. If the AMI filter finds nothing, list names with: aws ec2 describe-images --owners amazon --filters 'Name=name,Values=Deep Learning Base*Ubuntu 22.04*' --query 'Images[].Name'
expect: `terraform apply` then `aws ssm start-session --target $(terraform output -raw id)`, `sudo -iu ubuntu`, `nvidia-smi` shows your GPU. If spot capacity is not available, try another AZ (change subnet index) or another type.

title: Terraform: two EFA nodes (environment G2N) - only when you reach E2/F2
why: Copy infra/gpu1 to infra/efa2 and change: count = 2, instance_type = g4dn.12xlarge (supports EFA - confirm in the EC2 'EFA supported instance types' doc), a cluster placement group, and an EFA network interface instead of subnet_id/vpc_security_group_ids. EFA also needs the security group to allow all outbound traffic to itself - the rule below covers it. On-demand is safer than spot for multi-node. Two g4dn.12xlarge = 96 vCPU, so raise the On-Demand G and VT quota to 96 first.
expect: Both nodes up; on each `fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM` lists the efa provider. Budget: run 2-3 hours, then `terraform destroy`.

title: The nightly teardown habit (most important rule)
why: GPU labs get expensive only when you forget them. End every session with this. Add it to your shell as an alias.
code:
# ~/.bashrc
alias labdown='for d in ~/gpu-lab/infra/*/; do (cd "$d" && [ -f terraform.tfstate ] && terraform destroy -auto-approve); done; \
 aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running --query "Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType]" --output table'

labdown   # should end with an empty table
expect: Empty table = nothing running = no bill. Check Billing > Bills the next morning for the first week until you trust it.

title: Free and alternative GPU access
why: Some labs need hardware AWS spot cannot give cheaply (MIG on A100/H100, NVLink/NVSwitch, InfiniBand). Options: NVIDIA LaunchPad (free, time-boxed curated labs - apply via nvidia.com/launchpad), NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute courses with hosted GPUs, hourly A100/H100 rental from GPU clouds (compare current prices), or a colleague's cluster. Mark in your notes which results came from borrowed hardware.
expect: A short list of 2 providers with current $/hour for 1xA100 and 1xH100, saved in notes/hardware-options.md.
